RIP was the first routing protocol to be used. It is interior and distance vector: routers tell each other which networks they know and how many hops away they are. That is its metric (hop count, maximum 15): the path with the fewest hops wins. It travels encapsulated in UDP.

  • Version 1 (RFC 1058): classful. It only states the network (the "network 10"), so it does not work with subnetting.
  • Version 2 (RFC 2453): classless. It advertises each network along with its mask.
RIP does not know the topology: it only knows how many hops away each network is according to its neighbors.

RA announces network A. R1 hears it, records "A at 1 hop", and passes it on through all its interfaces. R2 receives that message, records "A at 2 hops", and repeats the same.

R3 and R4 end up at the same distance: A at 3 hops.

But R3 also announces the network to R4: from that side A is 4 hops away. R4 picks the shortest path and keeps the other one just in case.
Each router adds one hop to what it is told and keeps the lowest metric.
What R4 records about network A

Every 30 seconds (a random value between 25 and 35) the router sends its complete routing table to its neighbors. This also serves to know whether the neighbor is still there.

  • If a route is not refreshed within 3 minutes (6 lost updates), its metric becomes infinity: it is unreachable, the link is considered down, and the neighbors are informed.
  • 2 minutes later, a cleanup mechanism deletes the entries with infinity metric from the table.
In RIP nobody announces that something went down: the silence gives it away, and that takes minutes.

• Initialization: on startup it sends a broadcast request to all neighbors asking for their complete tables. It does no neighbor discovery and gets no acknowledgment.
  • Reliability: based on periodic retransmission.
  • Subnets (v2): includes the subnet information and advertises it in the updates.
  • Security (v2): optional 16-byte password, in cleartext. It prevents black-holes: routers that advertise all networks with metric 0.
Without the password, any router that advertises all networks with metric 0 becomes the best path for its neighbors: traffic goes toward it and is lost.

OSPF (RFC 2328) is the recommended interior protocol for TCP/IP: more robust and solid. It is link state and uses the Dijkstra algorithm.

Instead of passing along the table with its metrics, it internally builds a graph of the topology: it can see, beyond the directly connected neighbors, which is the best of the paths.

It considers more information than hops (for example bandwidth) and runs directly over IP, not over UDP.
The shortest path in hops is not always the best: OSPF can choose the one with more bandwidth.
RIP only counts hops: it picks the direct 64 kbps link. OSPF knows the whole graph and the state of each link: it goes through R2.

OSPF neighbors have an adjacency. When a router detects that an adjacency was lost (the neighbor is no longer reachable), it triggers a topology change notification that reaches all nodes.

  • Flooding: it floods the network with the notification and receives acknowledgment that it was received.
  • It exchanges less information than RIP: between one change and the next only keep-alives travel, which verify that the adjacent neighbor is still active.
RIP repeats everything every 30 seconds; OSPF advertises only when something changes, and does so right away.
Each router that receives the notice recomputes its graph. There is no need to wait minutes of silence as in RIP.

OSPF is hierarchical: it allows building areas connected to a backbone area.

Since it requires more storage and computation than RIP, it is best to keep areas small:

  • Routers in the same area exchange detailed topology information.
  • One of them talks to the backbone and exchanges summarized information.

The backbone consolidates and distributes. This scales far beyond RIP's 15 hops.
Detail inside the area, summary toward the outside: not everyone has to talk to everyone.
Autonomous systems: IGP inside, BGP4 between them

An IGP (Interior Gateway Protocol) such as RIP or OSPF runs inside one administrative domain, one company: an autonomous system. In there, you want every router to know the whole network.

To connect autonomous systems to each other, exterior protocols are used, for example BGP4.

When connecting to someone else's network I do not want to show them my whole topology, only what I want them to see. This is how Internet routing works.
Interior = all the information inside my organization. Exterior = only what I choose to publish.
RIP and OSPF, side by side

Both are interior and dynamic, but they solve the problem in very different ways.

RIP is simple and uses few resources, at the cost of converging slowly and not going past 15 hops.

OSPF needs more memory and computation, but chooses better, converges fast, and scales with areas. It also allows load balancing between two routes of equal metric, supports VLSM and CIDR, and can authenticate with a simple password or with hashing of the messages (MD5, preshared key) to guarantee integrity.
OSPF is a more complex process than RIP: it requires more storage and computation in each router. That is why it is best to keep areas small.
RIP and OSPF at a glance

• RIP: distance vector, metric in hops (max. 15), over UDP. v2 adds mask and password.
  • Full table every 30 s; 3 min with no news → infinity; 2 more min → deleted.
  • OSPF: link state with Dijkstra, over IP. Flooding of changes with acknowledgment and keep-alives.
  • Areas with detail inside and summary toward the backbone.
  • IGP inside the autonomous system; BGP4 between them.
